title: Q-learning with Coupled Reward Machines for Unordered Tasks
claim: A concrete task instance and its compact automaton-style reward specification show how an unordered multi-subtask goal is formalized.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; grid world beside a three-state automaton with labeled transitions
description: Panel (a) is a small black-bordered grid world with a 3-column by 4-row layout. It holds two boxes labeled b1 (top-left) and b2 (bottom-left), a station s (top, middle), and an agent A (right, second row). Panel (b) is a finite-state reward machine drawn as a graph with three circular nodes, u0, u1 and u2, in a row. An incoming arrow points to u0, and u2 is a double circle marking the accepting state. Arrows carry labels in angle brackets, each pairing a logical condition with a reward. Conditions use the station feature s and the numeric box feature b (b!, b-down, b-down-bar). u0 and u1 have self-loops. u0 and u1 are linked in both directions. The u1→u2 edge is labeled with reward 1. Everything is black on white, with (a) and (b) captions below.
caption: (a) Example Delivery instance with agent A, station s, and two boxes b$_1$ and b$_2$. (b) Numeric reward machine (RM) for the Delivery domain. A discrete numeric variable counts the number of uncollected boxes and is mapped to numeric feature $b$. Here, $b\dec$ is true when a box is collected, $b\decbar$ is true when all boxes are collected, and $b$! is true when not all boxes are collected. Boolean feature $s$ is true when the agent arrives at the station. The agent receives a reward of $1$ upon delivering all boxes to the station and $0$ otherwise.
abstract: Reward machines (RMs) inform reinforcement learning agents about the reward structure of the environment, enabling support for non-Markovian tasks and improving sample efficiency. However, learning with RMs is ill-suited for long-horizon tasks where subtasks can be completed in any order because learnt information grows exponentially with the number of such subtasks. To address this, we introduce $Q$-learning with coupled RMs (QCoRM), a task-decomposition algorithm that learns one low-level policy per subtask and a high-level policy over their completion order. In QCoRM, learnt subtask-level information increases only linearly with the number of unordered subtasks, and we theoretically show that the global optimality guarantee of tabular $Q$-learning is preserved. To enable QCoRM, we introduce agenda and coupled RMs: agenda RMs identify mergeable task-progression states, and coupled RMs enable subtask-level policy sharing. We also introduce numeric RMs for compact task representation. Our experiments across four domains---featuring both discrete and continuous action and state spaces---demonstrate that QCoRM scales to more unordered subtasks than baseline algorithms.
